Goeth
gō'eth
v. (third person singular present of go; rendering Hebrew halak and yatsa', Greek hupagei and ekporeuetai)
From Saxon gæþ, the third person singular present of gan, to go. It is the older goes, and in Scripture it is frequently paired with forth to describe an army, a whirlwind, or a word issuing out from its source.

Biblical Definition

Goeth is the older goes, and Scripture uses it for two very different motions. The first is the settled course of a life, especially a bad one: “the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses” (Psalm 68:21). The phrase describes not a fall but a walk — sin continued in, deliberately, after warning. The second is the going forth of something sent: “When the host goeth forth against thine enemies, then keep thee from every wicked thing” (Deuteronomy 23:9), where Israel's army on campaign is put under a stricter holiness than at home, because the LORD walks in the midst of the camp. Jeremiah uses the same construction of judgment: “the whirlwind of the LORD goeth forth with fury” (Jeremiah 30:23). And the Lord names a class of affliction that yields only to a particular discipline: “this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17:21). The verb is plain, but where it falls it usually marks either a persistence that will be judged or a power that has been dispatched.

Webster 1828 Definition

The third person singular of the present tense of go; the older form of goes. In Scripture it marks the settled course of a life continued in sin, and, with forth, the sending out of an army, a whirlwind of judgment, or a word from God.

GOETH, v. [Sax. gæþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of go; contracted in modern usage to goes.

2. To move; to pass; to proceed from one place or state to another.

3. With forth, to issue; to be sent out; as, the word goeth forth.

4. To walk; to be habitually engaged in a course; as, he goeth on in his trespasses.

5. In Scripture, such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses, Psa. 68; this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting, Matt. 17.

Key Scripture

Psalm 68:21 — "But God shall wound the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses."

Deuteronomy 23:9 — "When the host goeth forth against thine enemies, then keep thee from every wicked thing."

Jeremiah 30:23 — "Behold, the whirlwind of the LORD goeth forth with fury, a continuing whirlwind: it shall fall with pain upon the head of the wicked."

Matthew 17:21 — "Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting."

Modern Corruption

Persistent, deliberate sin is now widely reclassified as identity or as an unhealthy pattern to be managed, rather than as trespass continued in against light. Scripture's category is a man who goeth on still — a walk, chosen and repeated, for which he is answerable.

expand to see more

Therapeutic language has largely replaced moral language for habitual sin, and the replacement is not neutral. To call a besetting sin a pattern, a struggle, or a wound relocates it from the will to the circumstances, and where there is no agent there can be no repentance. Scripture is more honest and, in the end, more hopeful: it names the thing as trespass, holds the man responsible, and then offers a remedy that actually addresses guilt. A sin managed is a sin retained; a sin confessed is a sin forgiven.

The graver form of the error makes the sin an identity, so that turning from it would be a betrayal of the self. Scripture never permits that reasoning. It speaks of what men were — and such were some of you: but ye are washed — and treats the old life as something put off like a garment. Psalm 68:21 is deliberately severe because presumption is the last stage before judgment, and the man in view is not the one who stumbles but the one who has decided. The severity is mercy, since a warning is only useful while there is time to heed it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew halak is to walk or go, and is the standard metaphor for the moral course of a life; yatsa' is to go out or forth, used of armies and of the word of the LORD; Greek uses hupago and ekporeuomai.

expand to see more

Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, to go; the standing biblical figure for the whole course of a man's life.

Hebrew yatsa' (H3318) — to go out or forth; used of the host going to war and of the word going out of God's mouth.

Hebrew 'asham (H817) and pesha' (H6588) — guilt and trespass; what the persistent man goes on in.

Greek ekporeuomai (G1607) — to go out, to proceed from; used of what issues from the heart and the mouth.

Saxon gæþ — the Old English third singular present of gan, to go.

Usage

"Of sin persisted in after warning: such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses (Psalm 68:21)."

"Of holiness required of an army in the field: When the host goeth forth against thine enemies (Deuteronomy 23:9)."

"Of an affliction that yields only to a particular discipline: this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting (Matthew 17:21)."
